“Call for more action on climate change
 
Proposed
by Councillor Mike Massimi
Seconded
by Councillor Andreas Kirsch
 
This
Council notes:
(i)  the extraordinary heatwave in
Europe which has shattered numerous temperature records and had
major impacts on human health, ecosystems, agriculture,
infrastructure and labour productivity;
(ii)  the temperature recorded for
three consecutive days, with 37.3 °C recorded in southern
England on 25 June along with the Met Office’s Red Warnings
for Extreme Heat – the first time in the history of the
current weather warnings system that red warnings have been issued
for three consecutive days (which comes just weeks after May also
saw daily temperature records broken;)
(iii)  Kingston Council declared a
Climate Emergency in June 2019. 
'Kingston's Climate Action Strategy 2024 - 2030' recognises the
urgency of taking action to address climate change by reducing
emissions, protecting and enhancing nature and prepares the borough
for the unavoidable impacts of climate change, while also bringing
other benefits such as safer streets, healthier homes, new jobs and
improved air quality; and
(iv)  the vote in the House of
Commons last month to back a stricter, long-term climate target,
setting the Seventh Carbon Budget to reduce emissions by 87% by
2040.
This
Council believes:
(i)
The warning signs are mounting, Kingston Council is on the front
line of the climate crisis because the borough faces severe local
risks—like frequent flooding and extreme heat—while
concurrently holding the direct responsibility to protect
vulnerable residents, manage localised infrastructure, and reduce
emissions to achieve net-zero targets by 2038.
(ii)  the council cannot tackle
climate change alone.  Kingston Council
faces severe budget constraints primarily due to skyrocketing
demand for statutory services, particularly adult and children's
social care and massive cost increases in providing temporary
housing for the homeless;
(iii)  local authorities are best
placed to lead on community-based solutions, from retrofitting
homes to building public transport infrastructure and supporting
sustainable land use;
(iv)  the government holds the power
of financial initiative for climate change and we must urgently
secure and deliver the capital required to make an actionable
difference; and
(v)  the financial challenges
associated with tackling climate change are not unique to Kingston.
A recent report commissioned by the Mayor of London outlines an
ambition for the whole of London to be net zero by 2030. In that
report, there is reference to c£75b of funding required to
meet that level of ambition and at this time that funding has not
been identified or confirmed.
This
Council resolves to:
(i)  lobby the government to increase
funding for councils as a matter of urgency so that we can make
decisions that protect our residents and write to the new Minister
for Housing, Communities and Local Government and to The Secretary
of State for Energy Security and Net Zero pointing out: 
·        
Kingston Council’s budget restraints and
challenges;
·        
The need for more climate change funding
for:

§ 
(list as set out in the Heat Ready London
Policy)

§ 
the built environment

§ 
business and economy

§ 
emergency preparedness, resilience and
response

§ 
health and care

§ 
green space and nature

§ 
infrastructure
·        
the costs and risks of inaction have never been so
clear, with communities across the world being impacted by
flooding, heatwaves, food shortages and droughts;
·        
concerns that as more climate delivery is devolved
to councils and mayors, funding has not kept pace and will not keep
pace going forward, leaving a widening gap between net-zero
ambition and local delivery capacity; and
·        
concerns that, regardless of the ownership model
ultimately adopted for energy and water infrastructure, continued
uncertainty over financing and cost of capital is delaying
investment decisions with direct consequences for local environment
delivery and energy bills.”

Motion 2 - Armed Forces Covenant
Proposed by Cllr James Giles
Jointly Seconded by Cllrs Stephen Evans and Ian George

“This Council notes
that:


The Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames first
signed the Armed Forces Community Covenant in June 2013, and
renewed that commitment by signing the Armed Forces Covenant on
Armistice Day, 11 November 2018.

The Armed Forces Covenant represents a promise that
those who serve or have served in HM Armed Forces, and their
families, should be treated with fairness and respect, and should
face no disadvantage in accessing public services.

Kingston is rightly proud of its Armed Forces
community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans,
cadets, military families and the wider network of organisations
and volunteers who support them.

The Council has committed locally to appointing
elected member Armed Forces Champions, identifying an officer
champion, being a forces-friendly employer, raising awareness among
staff and elected members, reviewing policies and procedures, and
reporting annually on progress under the Covenant.


This Council believes:


The UK Government’s commitment to further
extend the Armed Forces Covenant in law is welcome, and provides an
important opportunity to improve support for the Armed Forces
community across public services.

However, legal duties alone will not deliver the
Covenant promise unless public bodies are given clear statutory
guidance, adequate funding, effective promotion, and proper
monitoring and accountability.


This Council resolves to:


Write to the Minister for Veterans and People,
Calvin Bailey MBE MP, in support of the Royal British
Legion’s “Keep the Covenant Promise”
campaign.

Call on the UK Government to provide improved
statutory guidance and sufficient funding to all public bodies
within scope of the extended Covenant Duty, including local
authorities, so that they can deliver better and more consistent
support for the Armed Forces community.

Ask the UK Government to implement a dedicated
programme of promotional activity on the Armed Forces Covenant, to
improve public awareness and positively recognise those who serve,
or have served, in HM Armed Forces.

Call on the UK Government to ensure that the impact
of the expanded Covenant Duty is thoroughly monitored, with clear
reporting on outcomes for the Armed Forces community.

Ask that members of the Armed Forces community are
given effective means of redress where the Covenant Duty is not
fulfilled.

Request that the relevant committee receives an
update on Kingston’s own delivery of the Armed Forces
Covenant, including awareness among staff and councillors, support
available locally, progress against previous commitments, and any
further steps needed to strengthen Kingston’s role as a
forces-friendly borough.”

Motion 3 - Every Councillor for Every Kind
Proposed by Cllr Yvonne Tracey
Seconded by Cllr James Giles
“Council notes the “Every Councillor for
Every Kind” Local Government manifesto produced by the RSPCA
and that local authorities have a significant role to play in
animal welfare through the various responsibilities we
have.
Council policy can protect domestic pets, livestock
and wildlife. Positive policy interventions can include
strengthening animal breeding license compliance, improving stray
dog services, serving high welfare food in council premises,
banning the use of snares, gluetraps and harmful netting on council
land, timing maintenance to not disturb nesting and hibernating
wildlife and improve reporting and investigation systems for animal
welfare concerns.
The RSPCA manifesto is split into 5
missions:

·        
Protect Pets and Promote Responsible Pet
Ownership

·        
Raise Welfare Standards for Farm
Animals

·        
Safeguard Wildlife Welfare and Natural
Habitats

·        
Enforce Animal Welfare Laws
Effectively

·        
Build Partnerships to Create Lasting
Impact
Council resolves to set up a Task and Finish Panel to
assess council performance against the 5 missions of the RSPCA
Local Government Manifesto and to create a list of recommendations
to be presented to the relevant strategic committee(s) to improve
animal welfare through council services.”
Motion 4 - Protecting Patients Prescribed
Cannabis-Based Products for Medicinal Use
Proposed by Cllr James Giles
Seconded by Cllr Yvonne Tracey

“This Council notes
that:


Cannabis-based products for medicinal use, known as
CBPMs, have been legally available under prescription in the UK
since 1 November 2018.

CBPMs may be prescribed, where clinically
appropriate, by specialist doctors for a range of conditions,
including some chronic pain, neurological, psychiatric, palliative
care and other long-term health conditions.

Many of the conditions for which CBPMs may be
prescribed can amount to disabilities under the Equality Act 2010,
depending on their impact on a person’s day-to-day
life.

Patients prescribed CBPMs should not be treated as
though they are using illegal or recreational cannabis when they
are using medication lawfully prescribed to them.

CBPMs may be prescribed in oil form, which is taken
orally, or in flower form, which is administered through a medical
vaporiser. Prescribed cannabis flower is not legally
smoked.

A medical vaporiser is distinct from smoking tobacco
or using a nicotine vape. It does not involve combustion and is
used by some patients to administer prescribed medication when
symptoms arise.

There remains a lack of public awareness about the
legal position of prescribed medical cannabis. This can leave
patients vulnerable to misunderstanding, stigma, inappropriate
enforcement, or discrimination when accessing services, housing,
employment, public buildings or licensed premises.

The Council has duties under the Equality Act 2010,
including the Public Sector Equality Duty, and should ensure that
its policies, services and frontline practice properly recognise
the needs of disabled residents and lawful users of prescribed
medication.

Kingston Council’s own Equality Impact
Assessment process exists to help ensure that council projects,
policies and service changes do not discriminate against people
with protected characteristics.

The Council’s role as a housing landlord,
licensing authority, employer, service provider and community
safety partner means it is well placed to improve local
understanding of CBPMs and prevent avoidable
discrimination.


This Council believes that:


No resident should be excluded from council
services, council premises, housing support, employment, community
facilities or licensed venues simply because they lawfully use
prescribed medication.

Reasonable and proportionate arrangements should be
made where a resident, employee or visitor needs to administer
prescribed medication, while also taking account of the comfort,
safety and needs of others.

Patients prescribed CBPMs should not be forced into
smoking areas to take prescribed medication, particularly where
this may expose them to tobacco smoke or undermine their dignity,
privacy or health.

Council officers, councillors, housing staff,
licensing teams, community safety partners and local providers
should have clear information about the distinction between
unlawful cannabis use and the lawful use of CBPMs under
prescription.


This Council therefore resolves
to:


Ask the Chief Executive to ensure that relevant
council services are made aware of the legal status of CBPMs and
the need to avoid discrimination against patients who lawfully use
prescribed medication.

Request that guidance is prepared for frontline
staff, including customer services, housing, community safety,
licensing, facilities management and HR, explaining what CBPMs are,
how they differ from unlawful cannabis use, and how reasonable
adjustments should be considered.

Ask officers to review policies covering council
premises, employment, housing management, anti-social behaviour,
licensing and community safety to ensure that they do not
inadvertently discriminate against residents, employees or visitors
who lawfully use prescribed CBPMs.

Ensure that Equality Impact Assessments for relevant
policies and service changes consider the needs of disabled
residents who may be prescribed CBPMs.

Ask that council-owned public buildings and
workplaces consider, where reasonable and practicable, how a safe
and appropriate space could be made available where a person needs
to administer prescribed medication.

Request that the Council’s licensing team
provides appropriate information to licensed premises in Kingston
about the legal status of CBPMs, the distinction between prescribed
medication and recreational cannabis use, and the need to avoid
unlawful discrimination.

Ask that any future local policies, Public Space
Protection Orders, byelaws or guidance relating to smoking, vaping,
anti-social behaviour or public spaces are drafted carefully so as
not to inadvertently capture the lawful use of prescribed
CBPMs.

Write to the Metropolitan Police South West Basic
Command Unit to ask what information and training is provided to
officers regarding prescribed CBPMs, lawful possession, medical
vaporisation, and the statutory medical defence in relevant road
traffic cases.

Write to registered providers and housing
associations operating in Kingston to ask them to confirm that
their housing management and anti-social behaviour processes
recognise the legal position of CBPMs and do not discriminate
against tenants who lawfully use prescribed medication.
Request that the People Committee receives a report
within six months setting out the steps taken, any policy changes
required, and any further work needed with health partners, housing
providers, police, licensed premises and disability
organisations.”

content:
The Council received a report and
recommendations on the new Local Plan following its consideration
by the Place Committee on 16 June 2026. The report sought approval
to undertake a statutory public consultation (Regulation 19) in
line with the Council’s Local Development Scheme 2026. The
consultation was proposed to run from 6 July 2026 to 4 September
2026.
 
Members noted that the new Local Plan covered
the period 2028-2043 and would replace the 2012 Core Strategy and
the Kingston Town Centre Area Action Plan and sought to deliver
nearly 20,000 homes to meet the Borough’s identified needs,
aligning with the 2024 National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF)
and the 2021 London Plan. This included optimising land use and
reviewing Green Belt/Grey Belt boundaries to meet housing
targets.
 
Members considered that following
consultation, the Council aimed to submit the Local Plan for
examination in December 2026, with an expected adoption in
2027/28.
 
Councillor Andrew Wooldridge moved a motion to
approve the Draft Local Plan for Regulation 19 consultation, as set
out in the supplementary pack which was seconded by Councillor
Andreas Kirsch. Members encouraged public engagement through the
consultation to be conducted on Regulation 19.
 
Following debate, it was RESOLVED that
–
 

1.   
the ‘publication document’ for Regulation 19 statutory
public consultation be approved, and officers be authorised to
proceed to Regulation 22 (submitting the Local Plan to the
Secretary of State and to notify the public of the submission),
subject to no major modifications arising from the Regulation 19
statutory public consultation:
 
a.   
Publication draft Local Plan (Annex 1);

 
b.   
Policies map (Annex 2);
 
c.   
Integrated Impact Assessment (IIA) Technical Note (Annex 3, to
follow as Late Material); and
 
d.   
 Statement of Consultation (Regulation
18) (Annex 4); and;
 

2.   
authority be delegated to the Director for Planning and
Regeneration, in consultation with the relevant Portfolio Holder,
to make any final amendments, additions and/or deletions to the
documents set out in Annex 1 and 2 of the report as they consider
reasonably necessary prior to public consultation.
 
Voting:
 
For:
Councillors: Sue Ansari, Brian Austen, Kim
Bailey, Joanne Barker, Mark Beynon, Emily Davey, Lorraine
Dunstone, Mark Durrant, Stephen Evans, Sam Foulder-Hughes, Helen Grocott, Sabah Hamed, Roger Hayes, Lesley Heap,
Peter Higgins, Amir Khan, Robert Kim, Andreas Kirsch, Griseldis Kirsch, Rizwana Malik, Ian Manders, Mark Manners, Mike Massimi, Helen Milestone, Sharukh Mirza, Callum
Morrissey, Nicola Nardelli, Elizabeth Park, Tom Reeve, Robert

and Yvonne Tracey. (3)

content:
The Committee received a report which set out
the proposed arrangements for the establishment and chairing of
Licensing Sub-Committees.
 
The Committee noted that the Licensing Act
2003 (Section 9(1) and 10(1)) required that the Licensing Committee
must meet to establish its Sub?Committees.
 
Consequently, the Licensing Committee was
convened on the rising of the Annual Council meeting to consider
the appointment of its members to Licensing Sub-Committees and the
arrangements for chairing those meetings. That was to ensure
minimal delay in convening a Sub?Committee should it be required
early in the new Municipal Year, given that licensing hearings must
be convened within statutory timescales.
 
The arrangements for Sub-Committee meetings
proposed in the report were in accordance with those introduced in
2012/13 (which have since then been agreed unanimously by the
Licensing Committee) as follows:
 
•     
Membership: Licensing Sub-Committees to be formed by drawing three
Members from the full pool of the membership of the Committee
(i.e. 15 Members)
•     
Chairing: Chairs would be appointed at each Licensing Sub-Committee
meeting
•     
Attendance: Each Member of the Committee is requested to fairly
share the responsibility for attendance across the full membership
of the Committee
 
The Clerk noted the need of some Members to
receive Licensing training before they participate in hearings, and
would convey that to Licensing Team officers for arrangement of
training at the earliest opportunity.
 
RESOLVED that the same arrangements for
the establishment and chairing of Licensing Sub-Committees, as
agreed by the Committee each year since 2012/13, set out in
paragraphs 5-8 of the report) be approved for the 2026/27 Municipal
Year.
 
Voting – Unanimous
topline: The Licensing Committee has decided to approve the arrangements for the establishment and chairing of Licensing Sub-Committees for the 2026/27 Municipal Year.

content:
The Council considered the recommendations of
the Licensing Committee held on 10 February 2026 on the outcome of
the consultation on the draft revised Statement of Licensing Policy
under the Licensing Act 2003, and the revised Policy for
2026-203. 
 
Members noted that, as a Licensing Authority,
the Council was required to prepare, at a minimum of every five
years, a Statement of Licensing Policy setting out its approach to
licensing and how that would inform and influence its decisions on
individual licence applications. The previous Statement of
Licensing Policy was approved by the Council in July 2021.
 
The Council noted that the revised draft
Statement of Licensing Policy incorporated several key updates. It
reflected current best practice and legislative changes, and
integrated new guidance concerning public health and
counterterrorism. Emerging issues, such as those highlighted in the
House of Commons Home Affairs Committee Report on spiking, were
also addressed. Additionally, the policy addressed the growing
concerns regarding safety and nuisance arising from the increasing
use of delivery services by licensed premises.
 
RESOLVED that the revised Statement of
Licensing Policy for 2026-2031, attached at Annex 1 of the late
material be adopted by the Council.
 
Voting: Unanimous
topline: The Licensing Committee has decided to adopt the revised Statement of Licensing Policy for 2026-2031, incorporating updates on public health, counterterrorism, and safety concerns related to licensed premises.

content:
The Council considered the Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2030 and the
2026/27 Detailed Budget, as recommended by the Corporate and
Resources Committee. Introducing the report, Councillor Richard
Thorpe (Portfolio Holder for Finance) highlighted a backdrop of
rising demand for social care and a £1bn funding gap across
London authorities.
 
The 2026/27 budget included:
£13.43m for service growth and demand (a
£3.93m increase over 2025/26).
£1.71m in new revenue savings, totalling
£3.43m when combined with previous commitments.
An average Council tax band of £2,097.61
at Band D (comprising a 2.99% general increase and a 2% Adult
Social Care precept).
£7.60m allocated to reserves for
inflation with the General Fund balance maintained at
£19.63m.
A four-year Capital Programme investment of
£248m (£142.93m General Fund; £105.07m HRA).
 
 
The Leader of the Opposition, Councillor James
Giles, proposed two amendments as set out in the Late Material Pack
(3). These were dealt with individually in accordance with the
Council’s procedural rules.
 
Amendment 1 –
moved by Councillor Giles and seconded by Councillor Chohan
 
In introducing the amendment, Councillor Giles
outlined concerns regarding the impact of permitted development
rights on the conversion of family homes into Houses in Multiple
Occupation (HMOs).
 
By way of response, the Leader of the Council,
Councillor Andreas Kirsch confirmed that the issue was already
being addressed through existing planning policy and officer
workstreams. Consequently, Councillor James Giles withdrew his
amendment.
 
Amendment 2 - moved
by Councillor Giles and seconded by Councillor Chohan
 
In introducing the amendment, Councillor Giles
explained that it sought to reallocate funding within the proposed
budget in order to prioritise core local services. Councillor Giles
expressed concern about council tax increases and the financial
pressures facing residents during the ongoing cost-of-living
challenges.
 
By way of response, Members emphasised the
complexity of the Council’s financial position, including the
need to manage borrowing costs, maintain statutory services and
plan for future financial sustainability. The debate also
referenced the national funding environment for local government
and the wider financial pressures affecting councils across
England.
 
Following the debate, Councillor Giles
requested a roll call vote under Procedure Rule 26 of the
Constitution. The Mayor put the
amendment to the vote and it was LOST.
 
Voting:
For: Councillors James Giles, Jamal
Chohan, Kamala Kugan and Yvonne Tracey (4)
 
Against: Councillors Afy Afilaka, Mark
Beynon, Andrew Bolton, Lorraine Dunstone, Mark Durrant,
Mariana Goncalves, Liz Green, Patrick Hall, Sabah Hamed, Roger
Hayes, Lesley Heap, Lynn Henderson, Peter Herlinger, Alison Holt, Amir Ali Khan, Robert
Dongsung Kim, Andreas Kirsch,
Griseldis Kirsch, Ian Manders, Mike Massimi,
Sharukh Mirza, Nicola Nardelli, Anne Owen, Elizabeth Park, Tom
Reeve, Farshid Sadr-Hashemi, Anita
Schaper, Susan Skipwith, John Sweeney,
Thay Thayalan, Richard Thorpe, Olly Wehring, Diane White, Andrew Wooldridge and
Yogan Yoganathan. (35)
 
Abstentions: Councillors Noel Hadjimichael and Sue Ansari. (2)
 
The Council returned to debate on the
substantive motion. Councillor Andreas Kirsch spoke in support of
the proposals. He highlighted the Council’s efforts to
maintain financial stability despite significant external pressures
and referenced positive external assessments of the Council’s
services. 
 
Councillor Kirsch and other Members expressed
appreciation for the work undertaken by officers in preparing the
budget and managing the Council’s finances. It was noted that
local authorities across the country were facing substantial
financial challenges and that the proposed budget sought to ensure
the continued delivery of services to residents while maintaining a
balanced financial position.
 
RESOLVED that –
 
1.       
the budget proposals and Council Tax for 2026/27 as set out in the
Budget Report Pack report and annexes be approved;
 
2.       
the relevant officers be authorised to take necessary action to
deliver the agreed budget and service charges, including increasing
relevant fees and charges in line with inflation or as recommended
within budget proposals;
 
3.       
in accordance with the requirements of the Local Government Act
2003, the comments of the Section 151 Officer in regard to the
robustness of estimates and the level of reserves and balances as
set out in the section “S25 Statement of Section 151
Officer” in paragraph 40 of the Budget Report Pack, be
noted;
 
4.       
in accordance with sections 32 to 36 of the Local Government Act
1992, the amounts in the statutory Council Tax calculation (Annex 3
of the Budget Report pack) for the financial year 2026/27, be
agreed;
 
5.       
the Capital Strategy including the detailed capital programme for
2026/27 to 2029/30 as set out in Annex 11 to the Budget Report, be
approved;
 
6.       
the Treasury Strategy including the Annual Investment Strategy,
prudential indicators and the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP)
policy as set out in Annex 12 to the Budget Report, be
approved;
 
7.       
the pay policy at Annex 13 to the budget report, be approved;
 
8.       
the Schools Budget for 2026/27 be approved in line with paragraph
20 and Enclosure 1 of Annex 14 to the Budget Pack;
 
9.       
the proposals outlined for the Central School Services Block be
approved (ref. para 31) of Annex 14 to the Budget Pack;
 
10.    
the proposals outlined for the Early Years Block be approved (ref.
paras. 32-38) of Annex 14 to the Budget Pack;

content:
After debate and amendments, the following
motion was put to the vote and CARRIED.
 
“This Council
notes:
 

·        
Gambling addiction is a growing national issue with a social cost
of over £1 billion a year.
 

·        
Harm from gambling affects families, public services and
communities, and is often concentrated in more vulnerable
areas.
 

·        
Kingston has a notable presence of betting shops and adult gaming
centres, with councils limited by outdated legislation –
particularly the “Aim to Permit” rule in the Gambling
Act 2005.
 

·        
Online gambling and widespread advertising have normalised
gambling, including among young people.
 

·        
A cross-council coalition, led initially by Brent, is calling for
urgent reform and has already influenced Government decisions on
machine regulation.
 

·        
The public overwhelmingly prefer high streets not dominated by
gambling premises.
 

·        
The number of premises licensed for gambling activity in the
Borough is declining but that online gambling that is not
controlled by the Council is increasing.
 
This Council
resolves to:
 
1. Support
national reform
 

·        
Join the coalition of councils calling for urgent gambling
reform.
 

·        
Endorse the Social Market Foundation High Streets at Stake
recommendations, including:
 
o  
Stronger local licensing powers and cumulative impact
assessments.

 
o  
Directors of Public Health involved in gambling licensing.

 
o  
Closing loopholes in gambling premises classifications.

 
o  
Raising the cap on licence fees to reflect enforcement costs.

 
o  
Clearer responsibilities between local authorities and the Gambling
Commission.

 
o  
Removing the “Aim to Permit” rule to restore local
democratic control.
 
2. Raise
Kingston’s voice nationally
 

·        
Write to the Secretaries of State for Culture, Media & Sport
and for Health & Social Care urging legislative reform.
 
3. Support harm
reduction
 

·        
Join and promote campaigns such as the Coalition to End Gambling
Ads (CEGA).
 

·        
Work with NHS, Public Health and voluntary sector partners to
improve signposting to gambling support and
education.”
topline: The Licensing Committee has decided to support national reform to address the growing issue of gambling addiction and harm in Kingston.

content:
After debate and amendments, the following
motion was put to the vote and CARRIED.
 
“This Council
notes: 
 
·        
The increase in Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) in our
borough, particularly in family residential streets, largely driven
by the ongoing housing crisis, affordability issues, and the need
for high-density, low-cost housing.
 
·        
That this expansion can change the nature of our communities.
 
·        
That many smaller HMOs can still be created without planning
permission under national permitted development rules, leaving
communities powerless to prevent the over-concentration of HMOs in
their area. 
 
·        
Kingston is already committed to taking decisive action, including
introducing Article 4 Directions, tighter planning policies, and
rigorous enforcement to protect their communities.
 
This Council
believes: 
 
·        
That residents have a right to live in safe, stable, and balanced
communities.
 
·        
That the current imbalance between landlord profit and resident
quality of life is unacceptable and the only way to redress the
balance is to build and buy more council housing moving the sector
from being a landlords market to a
tenants market. 
 
·        
That the unchecked spread increase of HMOs, in parts of the
borough, can reduce the balance in our communities. 
 
·        
That it is the Council’s duty to act swiftly and decisively
to increase the balance in our community.
 
Therefore, this
Council resolves to:
 
1.   Build more council homes.
 
2.   Instruct officers to continue to work on
implementing an Article 4
Direction. 
 
3.   Consult with communities to set strict
policies and thresholds in the Local plan relating to HMOs
including:
 

·        
restricting the concentration of HMOs in an area in particular on
both sides of a residential property

·        
ensure a good standard of accommodation and room size

·        
avoid an adverse impact on the neighbourhood ie on street parking
pressure

·        
insist on provision of cycle storage and refuse storage.
 
4.   Continuing to use the full strength of the
enforcement licensing and enforcement through the Anti social behaviour and private residential
enforcement teams.
 
5.   Ensure full public consultation with
residents on these measures, but commit in advance that this
Council will continue to prioritise protecting balanced communities
over landlord lobbying.
 
6.   To actively prepare for the Renters Rights
Act 2025 involving both landlords and tenants in preparation for
changes in rights and balance of power in particular the creation
of the Private Rented Sector database.
 
7.   Write to the Secretary of State demanding that the
government invest more in council housing.
 
8.   Request a report be brought back to the
relevant Committee within nine months to provide an update on the
progress on implementing Article 4 Direction.”
topline: The Council has decided to address the increase in HMOs by building more council homes, implementing stricter policies, and demanding government investment.

content:
RESOLVED that the following motion be
approved:
 

“Recognising the Contribution of Police Community Support
Officers

 

This Council notes:

·        
Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs) make an enormous
contribution to communities across Kingston, supporting
neighbourhood policing, improving visibility and building trusted
relationships with residents.

·        
PCSOs are often essential in mitigating the impact of police
abstraction — when warranted officers are pulled away from
neighbourhood duties for other pressures — helping maintain
consistent local presence and community reassurance.

·        
Despite this vital role, PCSOs are not eligible for the Police Long
Service and Good Conduct Medal awarded to police officers after
twenty years, and no equivalent national honour exists.

 

This Council resolves to:

·        
Support the national campaign for the creation of a long-service
medal for PCSOs, recognising those who dedicate 20 years to serving
and supporting our communities.

·        
Ask the Leader of the Council to write to the Home Secretary
endorsing the introduction of a formal decoration for PCSOs,
ensuring parity with police officers and acknowledging their role
in sustaining neighbourhood policing amid increasing operational
abstractions.

The Council considered a report from the Interim Director
of Governance and Law regarding the retention of the committee
system model of governance. Members noted in order to safeguard its
committee-based governance, the Council was recommended to pass a
resolution in response to the English Devolution and Community
Empowerment Bill, which would otherwise mandate a transition to a
Leader and Cabinet model. This action may secure a five-year
protection period for the current system, maintaining stable and
inclusive decision-making without requiring immediate financial or
operational changes.
 
The recommendation was moved by Councillor Andreas Kirsch and seconded by
Councillor James Giles.
 
RESOLVED that –
 

1.   
The Council would continue to operate a committee system form of
governance as permitted by section 9B(1)(b) of the Local Government
Act 2000.
 

2.   
That notice of this decision shall be made available for public
inspection at the Council offices and published in a newspaper
circulating in the local area.
 
Voting: Unanimous

content:
The Committee received a report on objections received
during the statutory Traffic Management Order reference Mapking0097
for Ewell Road Experimental Traffic Management Order
(ETMO).
 
The Committee noted that the new section of northbound
cycleway on Ewell Road between Langley Road and Oak Hill Crescent
was approved by the Place Committee on 14 March 2024. An ETMO
amending parking, loading and waiting restrictions on Ewell Road
came into force on 24 November 2024 and would be in force for a
maximum of 18 months. Under the ETMO, the loading bay was only for
goods vehicles loading, Monday to Saturday 8.30am to 6.30pm; and
parking was permitted in the bay, uncontrolled, outside of those
hours.
 
The Committee noted that, during the statutory
consultation, objections were received concerning the specific
arrangement and operational hours of the loading bay outside
140-142 Ewell Road. In response, officers recommended that the
objections be partially upheld and that the ETMO be made permanent
with amendment to the operating hours and waiting restrictions. The
revised use for the loading bay would be only for goods vehicles
loading, Monday to Sunday, midnight to 7am, 10am to 4pm and 7pm to
midnight, with a maximum stay of 30 minutes and no return within 2
hours. There would be no waiting or loading permitted in the
loading bay by any other vehicle at any time.
 
Four members of the public commented on the agenda item.
Two shop owners on Ewell Road spoke on the negative impact of the
removal of parking spaces and restrictions on using the loading bay
on their business. They considered that customers who used cars
were being discouraged from visiting their shops, and the Council
should consider providing some paid-for parking spaces in the roads
nearby the high street. Two other members of the public, including
a Kingston Cycling Campaign representative, were supportive to the
officers’ recommendations. They considered that the proposal
would facilitate cycling by reducing disruption to cyclists, and
support active travel. They were mindful that apart from car-users,
customers could also be cyclists and pedestrians.
 
Members of the Committee debated the recommendations by
officers. They were aware of comments and objections received, and
the ETMO arrangement in any case would be a compromise between
different stakeholders. A Member was inclined to provide more
flexibility for the use of the loading bay for the
businesses.
 
The Chair proposed an amendment, which was seconded by
Councillor Schaper, that (i) the words
“, and partially upheld” in recommendation 1 be
replaced by “and set aside”; and (ii) the words
“with a revision such that the loading bay operating hours be
restricted to those set out in paragraph 5 of the report” in
recommendation 2 be deleted. The amendment was equivalent to set
aside the objections received, and to make the ETMO permanent with
no revisions.
 
Members debated the amendment. In response to
Members’ questions, officers confirmed that the ETMO would
expire by the end of the 18-month period i.e. by 24 May 2026 if not made permanent (with or
without amendments). The Clerk advised the Committee that the last
meeting before the ETMO expiry would be held on 17 March 2026. Most
of the Members who spoke preferred to defer the decision on the
ETMO until parking data in the area affected by the ETMO was
available, which would require more time for officers to gather
data. A Member had expressed concern on the loss of funding from
TfL on the cycle lane project if that
was not completed.
 
The amendment was subsequently withdrawn by the
proposer.
 
Councillor Green moved a procedural motion, which was
seconded by Councillor Schaper, to defer the consideration of the
agenda item to a future meeting. The procedural motion was
carried.
 
Voting:

For:                    
Councillors Goncalves, Green,
Herlinger, Holt, Reeve, Schaper,
Thayalan, White, Wooldridge and
Yoganathan (10)

Against:             
Nil (0)

Abstention:
      
Councillor Manders (1)
topline: The Surbiton Neighbourhood Committee has deferred the decision on amending operating hours and waiting restrictions for a loading bay on Ewell Road.

content:
The Council debated a
motion which was submitted on behalf of
the Kingston Independent Residents Group, as proposed by Councillor
Jamal Chohan and seconded by Councillor
James Giles.
 
“Proposed by Councillor Jamal Chohan
Seconded by
Councillor James Giles
 
This Council
Notes:
1.   
The Pension Fund Panel’s decision on September 17th, 2025, to
review and strengthen the Responsible Investment Policy.
2.   
The Panel's commitment to consider international best practice,
noting that the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund model was discussed as an example.
3.   
The direct precedent set by other pension funds, such as the Danish
Teachers' Pension Fund (Lærernes
Pension), which have already divested from companies found to be
complicit in violations of international law in the Occupied
Palestinian Territories.
4.   
That other UK Local Government Pension Scheme pools, such as the
Brunel Pension Partnership, have adopted detailed responsible
investment policies that include specific commitments on human
rights, demonstrating a clear pathway for pooled funds to manage
these issues.

 
This Council
Believes:
 
1.   
That a strengthened Responsible Investment Policy, with clear and
robust exclusion criteria, is the most effective way to provide a
clear mandate to the London CIV and fulfil the democratic will of
the Full Council.
2.   
That this policy-strengthening work must be completed in a timely manner to maintain public confidence and
ensure prompt action.

 
This Council
Therefore Resolves To:
 
1.   
Mandate that the final, strengthened Responsible Investment Policy,
incorporating the principles of international best practice,
be presented to the Full Council for
formal approval no later than the December 2025 meeting.
2.   
Instruct the Pension Fund Panel to immediately
conduct a review to differentiate between its pooled fund
holdings and any segregated or directly held investments.
3.   
Asks the Panel, where any directly held or segregated investments
are found to be in companies on internationally recognised
exclusion lists (such as those published by the UN Human Rights
Office), to consider whether the process of divestment from those
investments should begin immediately, in line with a prudent,
'no-loss' sales policy.”
 
An amendment to the motion
was proposed by Councillor Andreas Kirsch and
seconded by Councillors Sabah Hamed on
behalf of the Liberal Democrat Group, so that it read as
follows:
 
“This Council
notes:
·        
the Pension Fund Panel’s decision on September
17th, 2025, to review and strengthen the Responsible Investment
Policy and its agreement, having identified its directly held
investments, to consider options to divest from and actively not
invest in companies on the UN OHCHR List;
·        
the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund model as an
example;
·        
the direct precedent set by other pension funds,
such as the Danish Teachers' Pension Fund (Lærernes Pension), which have already
divested from companies found to be complicit in violations of
international law in the Occupied Palestinian Territories;
and
·        
that other UK Local Government Pension Scheme pools, such as the
Brunel Pension Partnership, have adopted detailed responsible
investment policies that include specific commitments on human
rights, demonstrating a clear pathway for pooled funds to manage
these issues.

 
This
Council believes:
·        
that a strengthened Responsible Investment Policy,
with clear and robust exclusion criteria, is the most effective way
to provide a clear mandate to the London CIV and fulfil the
democratic will of the Full Council; and
·        
that this policy-strengthening work must be completed in a timely
manner to maintain public confidence and ensure prompt
action.
 
This
Council therefore resolves:
 
·        
that the final, strengthened Responsible Investment
Policy will be reported back latest at the 19th March Corporate and
Resources Committee and thereafter to the next meeting of Full
Council; and

 
·        
that the Pension Panel reports regularly on progress
on the recommendations of the Task and Finish group, agreed by the
Pension Panel on 17th September 2025 to the Corporate and Resources
Committee.

Motion (2):
 
COUNCIL MOTION FOR
REFERRAL TO PLACE COMMITTEE
 
“Motion on
Vehicle Crossover Policy
 
Proposed by Cllr
Yvonne Tracey
Seconded by Cllr
James Giles
 
This Council
notes:
 
1.   
That the Council’s current Vehicle Crossover Policy requires
applicants to demonstrate a minimum space of 3x4.6m to allow for a
crossover, which has led to a significant number of applications
being refused despite households having adequate space for safe
off-street parking.

 
2.   
That, in addition, many applications are being refused where grass
verges are deemed “too deep” beyond 2.0m, even when
safe and practical crossovers could be installed, resulting in
residents being unfairly denied access to off-street parking. This
has created disparities especially in Berrylands where deep grass verges are the
norm.
 
3.   
That, prior to 2019, rejected crossover
applications could be referred to the relevant Neighbourhood
Committee for determination by elected Members, ensuring democratic
oversight and local accountability.
 
4.   
That the current centralised decision-making process has removed
this layer of accountability and has led to frustration among
residents whose applications are refused
with no right of democratic recourse.
 
This Council
believes:
1.   
That crossover policy should balance highway safety with the
practical needs of residents, and that rigidly applying a 2-metre
depth maximum on grass verges or disallowing applications on the
grounds of short driveways does not always achieve this
balance.
 
2.   
That excessive restrictions based on verge width can unfairly
penalise households, particularly in parts of the Borough where
wide grass verges are common.
 
3.   
That enabling more residents to create off-street parking supports
the borough’s wider objectives, including:
 
4.   
Facilitating electric vehicle (EV) charging at home, thereby
helping to meet Kingston’s climate and air quality
commitments.
 
5.   
Reducing pressure on on-street parking, improving road safety and
accessibility.
 
6.   
Enhancing residents’ ability to transition towards more
sustainable transport in line with Council policy.
 
7.   
That decisions with a clear local impact
are best made locally, and that ward councillors and neighbourhood
committees are best placed to consider individual crossover
applications in the context of local circumstances.
 
8.   
That restoring Member oversight of disputed crossover applications
would improve public confidence in the fairness and transparency of
the system.
 
Therefore, this
Council resolves to:
 
1.   
Review and amend the policy on grass verges so that deep verges do
not automatically prevent residents from being
granted a crossover, where it is otherwise safe and
practical to do so, especially where many dropped curbs already
exist on a street with deep grass verges.

 
2.   
Reinstate within the policy an appeals process, especially where
the 3x4.6m requirement is the barrier, whereby rejected crossover
applications can be referred to the relevant Neighbourhood
Committee for final determination by elected
councillors.”
 
Motion (3):
 
COUNCIL MOTION FOR
REFERRAL TO CORPORATE AND RESOURCES COMMITTEE
 
“Committee
System versus Leader and Cabinet in Kingston
 
Proposed by
Councillor James Giles
Seconded by
Councillor Jamal Chohan
 
This Council
notes:
·        
The Minister of State for Local Government & English
Devolution’s characterisation of the committee system of
governance as being “unclear, duplicative, and
wasteful”.
 
·        
The government’s stated intention
to abolish the committee system and compel councils to adopt a
Strong Leader and Cabinet model.
 
This Council
believes:
·        
That the committee system provides clarity, accountability, and
inclusivity in local decision-making.
 
·        
That imposing a one-size-fits-all governance structure undermines
local autonomy and diminishes the democratic engagement of elected
representatives.
 
·        
That residents are best served when all
councillors are empowered to play a meaningful role in shaping the
future of their borough.
 
 
Therefore, this
Council resolves to:
·        
Oppose the government’s plans to abolish the committee
system.
 
·        
Continue to champion governance arrangements that put residents
first and empower all councillors.
 
·        
Communicate this position through writing a cross-party letter
(from the leaders of those groups willing to sign) to the Minister
of State for Local Government & English Devolution and to the
local MPs representing Kingston upon Thames.”
 
Motion (4):
 
MOTION FOR REFERRAL
TO CORPORATE AND RESOURCES COMMITTEE
 
“Amendment to
the Council Constitution – Member Call-In Threshold
 
Proposed by
Councillor Yvonne Tracey
Seconded by
Councillor James Giles
 
This Council
notes:
·        
The findings of the recent Local Government Association (LGA) Peer
Review into Kingston Council, which highlighted concerns regarding
the current threshold for member call-in of decisions.
 
·        
That under the current Constitution, nine elected members or
residents of the borough are required to call in a decision from
the Strategic Committee or a Neighbourhood Committee.
 
·        
That there are only six opposition councillors on Kingston Council,
which makes it impossible for the full opposition to exercise the
call-in mechanism without support from administration members.
 
This Council
believes:
·        
That effective scrutiny is a vital component of transparent,
accountable local democracy.
 
·        
That opposition councillors should have
a fair and realistic ability to exercise the constitutional right
of call-in, ensuring that decisions taken by the administration can
be subject to proper review.
 
·        
That aligning the call-in threshold with the total number of
opposition councillors will strengthen democratic accountability
and public confidence in the council’s decision-making
processes.
 
Therefore, this
Council resolves to:
·        
Amend the Council’s Constitution so that the threshold for
member call-in of a decision from the Strategic Committee or a
Neighbourhood Committee is reduced from
nine elected members to six elected members.
 
·        
Instruct the Monitoring Officer to update the Constitution
accordingly and ensure that the change is communicated clearly to
all members and relevant officers.”
 
Motion (5):
 
MOTION FOR REFERRAL
TO THE PLACE COMMITTEE
 
“Stopping the
Over-concentration of HMOs
 
Proposed by
Councillor Jamal Chohan
Seconded by
Councillor Yvonne Tracey
 
This Council
notes:
·        
The rapid and unchecked growth of Houses in Multiple Occupation
(HMOs) in our borough, particularly in family residential
streets.
 
·        
That this expansion is eroding community cohesion, driving up
antisocial behaviour complaints, intensifying parking and waste
problems, and placing significant pressure on local services.
 
 
·        
That many smaller HMOs can still be
created without planning permission under national permitted
development rules, leaving communities powerless to prevent the
over-concentration of HMOs in their area.
 
·        
That other local authorities have
already taken decisive action, using tools such as Article 4
Directions, tighter planning policies, and rigorous enforcement to
protect their communities.
 
This Council
believes:
·        
That residents have a right to live in safe, stable, and balanced
communities, not in streets dominated by transient, poorly managed
HMOs.
 
·        
That the current imbalance between landlord profit and resident quality of life is
unacceptable.
 
·        
That the unchecked spread of HMOs undermines family housing,
damages neighbourhood character, and risks hollowing out our
communities.
 
·        
That it is the Council’s duty to act swiftly and decisively
to stop the further erosion of our borough’s residential
areas.
 
 
Therefore, this
Council resolves to:

·        
Instruct officers to begin immediate work on implementing an
Article 4 Direction to remove permitted development rights for the
conversion of family homes into HMOs across the borough, and to
bring a report on the fastest possible timetable to the relevant
committee.
 

·        
Introduce strict saturation policies and thresholds in planning
policy, including maximum density limits and buffer zones to
prevent clustering of HMOs on individual streets.
 

·        
Strengthen licensing and enforcement by:
 
o  
Imposing tougher licence conditions on landlords covering noise, waste, antisocial
behaviour, and property standards.
 
o  
Increasing inspections and resourcing enforcement teams to ensure
compliance.
 
o  
Pursuing maximum penalties against rogue landlords, including licence revocation.
 

·        
Ensure full public consultation with residents on these measures,
but commit in advance that this Council will prioritise protecting
communities over landlord lobbying.
 

·        
Write to the Secretary of State demanding that government urgently
reform national planning laws so that all HMO conversions require
full planning consent and are subject to local democratic
control.”
